newsitem.title: INDIA: India expects "comfortable" wheat stocks in 97/98.
newsitem.headline: India expects "comfortable" wheat stocks in 97/98.

text.p: India's decision to pay bonuses to wheat farmers, plans to import the grain and the forecast of a bumper harvest will boost prospects of solid wheat stocks in 1997/98 (April-March), analysts said on Wednesday.

"The (state-fixed) prices have moved more close to the open-market prices which will help the government to procure more wheat from farmers and build comfortable stocks," M.S. Bhatia, adviser in the Agriculture Ministry, told Reuters.
The government buys wheat to build up its buffer stocks, which it then uses to control prices by releasing stocks through a state-run distribution system.
Indian government ministers on Tuesday agreed to pay a 600 rupee ($16.7) bonus per tonne to farmers for wheat it buys from them, in addition to the current purchase price of 4,150 rupees.
The bonus will be payable on the wheat offered for sale to the procurement agencies for the central pool up to June 10, 1997.
News agencies quoted Food Minister Devendra Prasad Yadav as saying the bonus will cost the government about seven billion rupees.
The cabinet has also decided to continue the ban of wheat and wheat products in 1997/98. India exported about two million tonnes of wheat in 1996/97.

Analysts said with better crop prospects, government agencies were expected to buy 10.2 million tonnes of wheat during the 1997/98 marketing season (April/March). They bought 8.2 million tonnes in the 1996/97 marketing season.
"In addition, exports are also banned for the current financial year," said a commodity analyst, who asked not to be identified. "This should make our stock position quite reasonable."

Minister Yadav told parliament earlier this week India's wheat stocks on April 1 were projected at 2.72 million tonnes, down one million tonnes from the buffer stock norms of 3.7 million tonnes set by the government.
India banned exports of wheat in September 1996 when stock limits fell to very low levels because purchases by state agencies were four million tonnes less than estimated.

In December, India authorised the state-run State Trading Corporation (STC) to import two million tonnes of wheat to build stocks and check rising prices. STC officials said it had contracted to import 1.7 million tonnes so far.
Analysts said the wheat harvest was in full swing in the central state of Madhya Pradesh and western state of Gujarat, and was picking up in the northern states of Rajasthan and Punjab.
The Agriculture Ministry has forecast the 1996/97 (July-June) wheat crop at 64.5 million tonnes against 62.6 million in 1995/96.

"As more wheat starts coming to the markets the prices will fall and I expect prices to fall below 6,000 rupees per tonne," the analyst said. "At the same time, the bonus will attract farmers to some extent to sell to the government."
The current open market sale price of wheat is around 6,000-6,500 rupees per tonne. It varies from state to state.

An official of the state-run grain procurement agency Food Corporation of India said it had not started buying wheat because the harvest in the northern states, the major wheat contributors, was not yet in full swing. ($1 = 35.8 rupees)
